newsitem.title: GERMANY: President says Germany needs foreign workers.
newsitem.headline: President says Germany needs foreign workers.

text.p: President Roman Herzog said on Tuesday Germany's economic strength was due in part to foreign workers and Germans were wrong to believe foreigners were taking away their jobs.

Speaking at the German opening of the European Year against Racism in Berlin on Tuesday, Herzog urged Germans to build bridges to people from the various international cultures who live and work in Germany.

The opening ceremony was disrupted by a group of guests who unfurled a banner in the middle of Berlin Mayor Eberhard Diepgen's speech, protesting against a recent government decision requiring the children of some foreigners to obtain visas. Many participants stood and applauded.
"It is wrong to say that foreigners are taking jobs away from Germans," Herzog said.

"It is wrong to say foreigners are living from welfare or in need of support here," he added. "Rather it is more the case that they have made considerable contributions to the economic success of Germany as workers and independent businessmen."

The European Year Against Racism, which has a budget of 4.7 million European currency units ($5.55 million), was opened in the Netherlands in January. The European Union is committed to fighting racial discrimination, xenophobia and anti-Semitism.

Germany faced a wave of racist violence following unification in 1990, particularly in the formerly communist east of the country. Commentators fear economic problems are leading to a new surge of racism.
Der Spiegel weekly magazine said the danger of a new wave of right-wing extremism was "a ticking timebomb".
Record unemployment of 4.66 million in January, not seen since Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933, has sparked accusations that foreigners have stolen jobs from Germans.

Mainstream politicians had long refrained from directly linking the high unemployment level to the country's eight million foreign residents, in part because they wanted to avoid being accused of fomenting racial unrest.

But in January Finance Minister Theo Waigel said it was "grotesque" that millions of Germans were unemployed while so many foreigners were working here. Several other conservative political leaders echoed Waigel's sentiment.
Groups protecting foreigners dismiss that contention, saying foreigners take many of the low-pay and menial jobs that Germans refuse to accept.
